e.t: This adjective means “wild”: something not domesticated, cultivated, or under ordinary human control. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes what is wild rather than familiar, settled, or managed. Its 23 occurrences span the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, showing a recurring description used across different passages. The surrounding verse determines what is being described, but the central idea remains the same: something belonging to a wild or untamed condition.

Ailath, also rendered Elath, is a proper name used in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs seven times in the LXX corpus, across five verses, from 1 Kings 9:26 through 2 Chronicles 26:2. Its exact significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and its setting.

Akiezi is a proper name, preserved in the Greek Old Testament as “Akiezi.” It functions as a specific name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at Joshua 15:44. The available information identifies the name and its location, but does not provide the surrounding verse text needed to explain whether it refers to a person, place, or another named entity in that passage.

Aloua, also rendered Alua, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Joshua 15:58. The name identifies a particular person or place in that passage, but the available wording here does not establish which one. Its meaning is therefore best represented by the name itself: “Aloua” or “Alua.” The surrounding verse would be needed to explain what this named entity refers to in context.

Amoris is a proper name, not a word describing an action, quality, or object. It functions as a name used to identify a particular named entity in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Genesis 14:13. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the passage itself is needed to determine whether Amoris refers to a person, place, or another named subject.

This word means “reading,” referring to the act of reading a written text. As a noun, it names the reading itself rather than a person who reads or a particular passage. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Nehemiah 8:8. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the activity of reading. The word therefore points to the presentation or reception of written words through reading.

This Greek LXX word describes mindlessness or witlessness: a lack of sound understanding or sensible thought. As a noun or adjective, it can identify such a condition or characterize someone or something marked by it. The word occurs 13 times in the Greek LXX, in both the Old Testament books and the deuterocanonical writings. Its basic sense points to deficient judgment or understanding, while the surrounding verse determines whether it describes a person, an attitude, or conduct.

This Greek LXX verb means to “hold side by side” or “compare.” It describes placing things alongside one another so they can be considered in relation to each other. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 23:12, though the surrounding verse text is not available here for explaining its particular use.

This verb means “report”: to pass information from one person to another. It describes the act of telling or making something known, whether the information concerns events, people, or other matters being communicated. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 220 times, making it a regularly used word for conveying a report. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is being reported and to whom.

This noun means “giving back; restitution”—the act of returning what is owed, due, or received. It points to repayment or restoration rather than simply possessing something. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice: once in Deuteronomy and once in Sirach. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and situation, but its central idea remains giving something back or making restitution. This word belongs to the Greek LXX tradition and should be understood within that corpus. [p03:word:lxx:L701453:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L701453:occurrences]

This Greek LXX verb means “send off/away.” It describes causing someone or something to go from one place to another, whether by sending, dismissing, or dispatching. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs 625 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, showing that sending is a recurring action in these texts. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on who is sent, where they go, and the surrounding context.

This adjective describes a person or possession acquired by payment in silver—that is, purchased with silver. It identifies how someone or something came to be obtained, rather than describing a character quality or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, all in Genesis and Exodus, where it is associated with people or household members acquired through payment. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains something obtained by silver payment.

This word means “original” or “ancient”. It is an adjective describing something belonging to an earlier time, existing from the beginning, or standing as an older source or tradition. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it occurs 26 times, including passages translated with “ancient.” Its meaning remains centered on age or priority rather than describing a particular event or spiritual quality by itself; the surrounding verse determines exactly what it describes. [p03:word:lxx:L701835:identity, p03:word:lxx:L701835:occurrences, p01:word:lxx:L701835:reference:0, p01:word:lxx:L701835:reference:5]

Archi, also given as Arkhi, is a proper name identifying a person rather than expressing a general quality or action. In the Greek LXX, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Samuel. The name appears in 2 Samuel 15:32 and 2 Samuel 16:16. Without the verse text, its specific role in those passages cannot be explained further, but its basic meaning is a personal name. It should therefore be read as a name, not translated as an ordinary descriptive word.

This adjective describes something that is “unsteady” or “unstable,” lacking firmness or dependable balance. It can characterize a person, condition, or situation that does not remain steady. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 5:39. The precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and paragraph, but the central idea remains a lack of stability or constancy.

Atar is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. The available meaning is simply “Atar”; the word itself does not provide a broader description such as a quality, action, or object. It occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, both times in Job, at Job 6:21 and Job 7:11. Identifying exactly whom or what Atar refers to requires the surrounding verse text and passage context.

Badiel is a personal name referring to an individual in the Greek Old Testament. The name is also given as “Vathil,” showing that these are recognized forms associated with the same named person. It functions as a proper noun rather than a general description, action, or spiritual quality. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Nehemiah 11:14. Without the surrounding verse text, its broader significance cannot be stated beyond identifying the person named there.

Baithangan, also rendered Vethanggan, is a proper name for a location. It is not a general description or action word, but the name of a specific place mentioned once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Kings 9:27. Because the word occurs only there and no verse text is provided here, its exact role in that passage must be understood from the surrounding account. The name itself identifies the place called Baithangan or Vethanggan.

Baraia is a personal name, also rendered “Varea.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 8:21. The available wording preserves the name itself, but the verse text and surrounding passage are needed to say more about the individual or the role he has in that passage.

This proper name refers to Bel, also given as Vil. It functions as a personal or divine name rather than a general description or action word. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 15 times: once in Isaiah and 14 times in Bel and the Dragon. The name is therefore especially associated with the figure called Bel in that latter work, while its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun means a throw or a shot—the act or result of sending something through the air. It can describe a cast or projectile movement rather than the object being thrown itself. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, including Genesis, 2 Maccabees, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and what is being sent. [p03:word:lxx:L702755:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L702755:occurrences]

Gersōn, also rendered Yirson, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action or quality. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, in Genesis 46:11, and the English rendering is Gerson. The name’s precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse text, but its basic function is to identify a person. This LXX occurrence should be kept distinct from similarly rendered names or source words in other biblical language traditions.

Gog is a proper name, rendered “Gog,” used for a named figure in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general description or ordinary action word, but a personal designation. This name occurs 14 times in the Greek LXX Old Testament, appearing most often in Ezekiel, with additional occurrences in Numbers and Amos. Its precise identity and role in any particular passage must be understood from that passage’s surrounding text.

Deseth, also rendered Theseth, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament (LXX), identifying a person or place rather than expressing an ordinary action, quality, or object. Its precise referent cannot be determined from the name itself. This name occurs once in the LXX, at Isaiah 16:7; the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain whom or what it identifies there.

This noun means “diagnosis”: a determination or identification of a condition or situation. It names the act or result of discerning what something is, rather than describing a person or action. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 3:18. The surrounding verse text is needed to show how the word functions in that particular sentence, but its basic meaning remains a diagnosis or clear determination. [Evidence: p03:word:lxx:L703437:identity; p03:word:lxx:L703437:occurrences; p01:word:lxx:L703437:reference:0]

This adjective means “two hundred.” It identifies a quantity of 200, usually describing a number of people, objects, or units in a larger statement. In this Greek-scripture corpus, it occurs 80 times, so it is a recurring numerical term rather than a rare or specialized expression. Its exact referent—what is being counted—comes from the surrounding sentence, but the number itself remains precise: 200.

This verb means “suspend” or “interrupt”—to stop something temporarily or prevent it from continuing. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at Numbers 23:19. As a verb, it describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic idea is a stopping, delaying, or breaking off of an action or process.

This Greek Old Testament adverb means “differently,” describing an action or manner that is unlike what has already been mentioned or expected. It answers the question “how?” by indicating a distinct way of doing or being. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Daniel 7:7. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage, but its basic meaning remains a contrast in manner: something happens in a different way.

This adjective describes someone who acts with fortitude—showing inner strength and firmness when facing difficulty or choosing a course of action. Its basic sense is “with fortitude,” and it occurs five times in the Greek LXX corpus, all within Wisdom and Sirach. Because the word is an adjective, it describes a person or quality rather than naming an action by itself. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

Egli is a proper name used to identify a person or named figure, rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, at Numbers 34:22. Because the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its specific role in that passage cannot be explained here. Its basic meaning is therefore the personal or proper name “Egli.”

This noun refers to an assembly—a gathering of people brought together for a shared purpose. In the Greek Old Testament, it commonly identifies the gathered community rather than one individual. Its basic meaning is consistent across its 95 occurrences in the LXX corpus, which includes both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. The word appears in passages connected with Israel’s gathered community, worship, and public life, though the precise force in any verse depends on its surrounding context.

This verb means “pick olives”—to gather olives from the tree. It describes an action rather than an object, so it functions as a verb in the Greek Old Testament. This word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Deuteronomy 24:20. Its central sense is clear, while the precise force of the action in that verse is best understood from the verse and its surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “embark” or “step in”—to move onto or into something, especially when boarding. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word occurs four times in the LXX corpus, appearing in Jonah, Nahum, 1 Maccabees, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on what the surrounding sentence says, but its central idea remains entering or getting aboard.

This noun refers to an informer or complainant—the person who brings information or a complaint forward. It identifies someone acting as a reporting or accusing party, rather than describing the information or complaint itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 4:1. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative context, which are not included here.

This verb describes causing irritation or trouble, and it can also describe someone being unwell or troubled. Its basic sense is that a person is affected unpleasantly—either bothered by something or suffering difficulty. The word appears four times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, so it is uncommon there. Its precise force in any one passage depends on whether the sentence focuses on annoying another person or on experiencing distress or illness.

This Greek LXX noun means “searching out” or “search”—the deliberate effort to look for something, investigate it, or seek to discover it. It describes the activity of pursuing understanding rather than the thing being sought. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, once in Isaiah and once in Baruch. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic sense remains an intentional search or investigation.

This verb means to “concede” or “confess”: to openly acknowledge something as true or admit it. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it can describe a person’s spoken acknowledgment, including confession directed toward God. The word occurs 103 times in this LXX corpus, so it expresses a recurring action rather than a rare or specialized idea. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “make manly.” It describes an action that causes someone to become manly, rather than naming a person, object, or abstract idea. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 15:17. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here; its basic lexical sense remains the action of making manly.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “rain upon”: it describes rain falling on or being sent down over someone or something. It is an action word, so it expresses what rain does rather than naming the rain itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 10:6. The exact force of that occurrence depends on the surrounding verse, but the word’s basic meaning remains the act of raining upon.

This adjective describes a person or thing as choice—something identified as selected or preferred. It functions as a describing word rather than naming an action or event. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 14 times across 14 verses, with most occurrences in Ezekiel and additional uses in Exodus, Joshua, Daniel, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the noun it describes and the surrounding passage.

This adjective means “perjured”—someone who has broken an oath or given false testimony under oath. It describes a person marked by unfaithfulness to a sworn promise, rather than simply someone who makes an ordinary mistake or tells an unintentional falsehood. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Zechariah 5:3. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a person who has violated an oath or sworn obligation.

This noun means “supervision” or “visitation”: the attentive oversight or coming of someone to inspect, care for, or deal with a matter. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, it can describe an overseeing presence or a significant visit, while the surrounding passage determines the precise force. The word occurs 41 times in this LXX corpus, showing that it is used across several kinds of passages rather than having only one narrow application. Its basic idea is purposeful attention directed toward people or circumstances.

This noun means “taskmaster” or “slave master”—a person who oversees and drives enslaved workers to perform assigned labor. It describes an authority figure connected with compulsory work rather than an ordinary supervisor. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament, especially in Exodus and also in 1 and 2 Chronicles. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Esri, also rendered Ezri, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual by name in the Greek LXX tradition. The name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 4:17. Since the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the name’s specific role in that passage cannot be explained beyond its identifying function.

This adjective describes someone or something as well-shaped or goodly—having an attractive, pleasing appearance. It is a descriptive word rather than a title or action, so its meaning focuses on outward form or visible quality. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Daniel 1:4. The surrounding verse is needed to know exactly whom or what it describes there, but the word itself points to an appealing or well-formed appearance.

This word means “handsomely” or “elegantly,” describing the manner in which something is done or appears. It functions as an adverb, so it adds the idea of beauty, grace, or pleasing form to an action or description rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 13:11. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and sentence, but its normal sense is doing or presenting something in a handsome, graceful, or elegant way.

“Revere” means to treat someone with deep respect and honor. As a verb, it describes an action of showing profound regard rather than merely noticing or acknowledging someone. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, this word occurs eight times, including in Isaiah, Sirach, 4 Maccabees, and Susanna. Its precise expression depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains reverent respect.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person named Elasa, also rendered Ilasa. It does not describe an action, quality, or object; it identifies an individual. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 10:22. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself gives no further information about the person’s character, role, or significance. Its basic meaning is therefore the personal name Elasa or Ilasa.

This Greek LXX verb means “amaze” or “wonder”: it describes a person being struck with amazement or filled with wonder. It is an action word, focusing on the response produced by something astonishing or extraordinary. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical corpus, it occurs four times, appearing in 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 2 Kings, and Wisdom. The precise force in any one passage depends on what causes the amazement and how the surrounding verse describes the response.

Thekōitis, also rendered Thekitis, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a particular person or place by name rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. In the LXX, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Samuel 14:4 and 2 Samuel 14:9. The name’s precise referent in each verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the lexical evidence identifies it as a proper name, not a common descriptive term.

This word means “furnaces,” referring to enclosed places or structures used for intense heating. It is a plural noun, so it describes more than one furnace rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 12:38. Without the surrounding verse text, the word itself gives the basic object being named, while the passage determines what kind of furnaces are meant and why they are mentioned.

This noun means a broken piece or fragment—something that has been broken off or left in pieces. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for a physical condition examined under the laws concerning skin disease and for related conditions of garments or surfaces. The word occurs 15 times, all in Leviticus, especially in chapters 13–14. Its central idea remains concrete: a piece or portion resulting from breaking, rather than a person’s character, an action, or an abstract state.

Iassa is a proper name used in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a particular person or place named Iassa, but the available information does not provide enough verse text to determine which in each occurrence. The name appears five times in the Greek Old Testament, in Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. Its meaning is therefore best understood as the name Iassa itself, while its specific referent depends on the surrounding passage.

Iemouath, also rendered Iemuath, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears only once, in 2 Kings 12:22. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s particular role in that passage cannot be explained further; its basic meaning is simply the individual’s name. The two forms identify the same named person in this LXX occurrence.

Iesbok, also rendered Iezvok, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This name occurs once in the LXX, at Genesis 25:2. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide an additional descriptive meaning or etymological explanation. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being named.

This Greek LXX verb means “establish” or “appoint”—to put someone or something into a recognized position, responsibility, or arrangement. It can describe setting a person over others or determining an order or place. The word occurs 198 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is broad and regularly used for acts of assigning or establishing. Its precise force in any verse depends on what or whom the surrounding passage says is being established or appointed.

This Greek LXX word means “down” or “by.” It is commonly used as a preposition, showing direction, position, or relation, and it can also function as an adverb. Its precise force depends on the words and sentence around it, but the central idea is movement or location in relation to something else. It occurs 1,936 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so it serves a broad and recurring role in the LXX.

This verb means “portion out”—to divide something into assigned shares or portions. It describes the act of distributing what is to be received, rather than simply possessing it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, all in 1 Samuel, including passages about selecting or assigning among people. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being divided and who receives each portion.

This Greek LXX verb means “press” or “urge.” It describes actively pushing someone toward movement, action, or a response rather than merely making a request. The word can therefore express forceful prompting or hastening, depending on the sentence. It occurs 20 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing a recurring sense of pressing someone or something forward. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being urged and the surrounding context.

This noun means “one who is in charge”—a person with authority or responsibility over others. It identifies someone by a governing or supervisory role rather than by a personal name or specific task. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 4:2. The verse’s surrounding wording would be needed to explain the particular responsibility intended in that passage.

This word means “collar,” a noun for something placed or worn around the neck. It names a physical object rather than an action or personal quality. In the LXX corpus, it occurs 21 times, showing repeated use across the Greek Old Testament and related Jewish Scriptures. Its exact force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central meaning remains a collar or neck-band.

This adjective describes something as “like ice,” pointing to an icy resemblance or quality. It is a rare word in the Greek Old Testament, appearing once in the Wisdom of Solomon, at Wisdom 19:21. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise reference in that passage cannot be explained further; its basic meaning remains a comparison to ice.

Kōlia, also rendered Kolia, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person named in Ezra and Nehemiah. The name occurs twice in this corpus, once in Ezra 10:23 and once in Nehemiah 11:7. Without the surrounding verse text, Scripture does not provide a broader lexical meaning for the name itself.

Lobna is a personal name, rendered as “Lobna” or “Lovna.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 6:42. The available wording establishes the name itself, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain the person’s specific place in that passage. Its meaning is therefore best understood as the proper name Lobna, also known as Lovna.

“Madbaritite” is a name or descriptive designation for someone or something associated with Madbar. In the Greek Old Testament, it functions as both a noun and an adjective, so it can identify a person or describe a related place, people, or belonging. This term occurs twice in the Greek text, both times in Joshua. Its exact reference in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This adjective means “long.” It describes something extended in length or duration, depending on the sentence, rather than naming an action or person. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented here, it occurs 12 times across 12 verses. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on what is being described, but its central idea remains length or extended duration.

Massē, also written Massi, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named individual or place, but the available lexical information does not specify which kind of name it is. The name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, in Genesis and 1 Chronicles, and is rendered “Masse” where an English rendering is available. Its exact reference in each passage depends on the surrounding verse context.

This Greek LXX noun means “boy” or “lad,” referring to a young male person. It is a straightforward word for a youth rather than a title, office, or abstract quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, all in 2 Maccabees and 4 Maccabees. The word’s exact force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its ordinary meaning remains a young boy or lad. It should be understood as a concrete description of a person.

This word means “mine,” referring to a place where valuable materials are extracted from the earth. It is a noun, so it names the site or resource rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 8:3. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the word’s exact emphasis in that sentence cannot be stated beyond this basic meaning.

“Bat” means the flying nocturnal animal identified by that name. In the LXX, this noun refers to a literal creature rather than an action, quality, or person. It occurs four times across the LXX, appearing in passages from Leviticus, Deuteronomy, Isaiah, and the Epistle of Jeremiah. The English rendering “bat” confirms the ordinary sense. When the word appears in a particular verse, its wider significance depends on that passage’s surrounding text.

This adjective means “slothful”: unwilling or slow to apply oneself with diligence. It describes a person marked by sluggishness rather than energetic effort. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times—once in Proverbs and twice in Sirach—so its central idea remains consistent across these occurrences. The surrounding verse determines whether the word emphasizes a person’s work, response, or general lack of initiative.

This word means “administer”: to carry out responsibility for managing or directing something. It functions chiefly as an action word, describing what a person does when entrusted with oversight. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it occurs three times, so its basic sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included. Its precise force in any one passage depends on what is being administered and on the wider context. The word appears once in Psalms and twice in Maccabees.

The word means “to see” or “to view”—to perceive something with the eyes or look upon it. It is a verb describing the act of seeing rather than a person or thing seen. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 513 times across the corpus, showing that it is a broadly used word for visual perception. The surrounding verse determines its precise force. Available English renderings use “see” most often and “view” less often.

This Greek LXX noun means “marking out by boundaries” or “limitation.” It refers to setting something apart by defining its limits, whether describing a boundary, a restriction, or a determined scope. The word appears 22 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books represented here, with especially frequent use in Numbers and Daniel. Its basic idea remains consistent: something is established or understood by the boundaries that mark it out. The precise force in any verse depends on what is being limited or defined there.

Urias is a proper name, rendered “Urias.” It identifies a person rather than expressing a general quality, action, or idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs 35 times across 31 verses, with many occurrences in 2 Samuel and additional occurrences in Exodus, 2 Kings, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. Because it is a personal name, the particular person identified depends on the surrounding passage; the name itself simply designates Urias. Its use begins in Exodus and continues through Jeremiah.

This word means “antiquity”. It is a noun referring to something belonging to a very distant past, including a “relic of ancient times.” In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, all in Job, so it is uncommon and carries a focused sense rather than serving as a broad everyday term. The word can point to the age or venerable character of something, while the surrounding passage determines what ancient thing is being described. Its meaning is centered on age, antiquity, and what comes from long ago.

This Greek LXX noun means “deposit,” referring to something placed with another person or entrusted to another’s care. It names a thing committed to someone, rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs twice, both times in Leviticus 5, at verses 21 and 23. The central idea is an entrusted deposit whose proper handling matters in the surrounding instruction. Its precise force in either verse depends on the actual passage context.

This verb means “make proverbial”: to turn something into a saying or memorable expression that can be repeated and recognized. It describes the act of presenting words or an event in a proverb-like form, rather than simply speaking about it plainly. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears once, in 4 Maccabees 18:16. The precise force of the verb in that sentence depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic idea is making something proverbial or expressing it as a proverb.

This verb means “shear,” describing the cutting or removing of hair or wool. It is an action word rather than a name or description of a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Jeremiah, so its ordinary meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. Its precise force in either passage depends on what is being sheared and how the action fits the surrounding sentence.

This adjective describes people or things that remain or survive after others are gone. It points to what is left over, still present, or preserved. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Psalms 20:13 and Amos 5:15. Its basic sense is straightforward: something or someone has endured and continues to exist. The surrounding verse determines whether the word emphasizes mere survival, the remnant that remains, or what is left after a larger group or collection has been reduced.

This verb means “fill” or “fulfill”: to make something full, bring it to completion, or cause a stated purpose to be carried out. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used broadly for things becoming full and for actions or conditions reaching their intended measure. It occurs 112 times in this corpus, so its precise force depends on what is being filled or fulfilled in the surrounding passage.

This word means to work in various colours or to embroider. It is a verb describing an action that produces a varied-colour result rather than naming a person or thing.
